prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for B027 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific arc is complete and independently confirmed, from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, through the physiology of secretion and receptor signalling, to agents with replicated outcome benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease. Nothing in the first round weakened that, and nobody argued that it is premature or contested on efficacy. The round also did not give me a reason to add a second part. A two-part prize would require cutting the GLP-1 credit below three, which would damage the strongest part to make room for a weaker one, and the chair's question about pairing a smaller GLP-1 configuration with another achievement has no workable answer under the three-person cap. I would rather have one clean, well-argued part than two uneven ones. I now make the citation wording more explicit: it should name the discovery of the physiology and the active form and say that this made incretin-based treatment possible, so it states the link to therapy without crediting drug design.
statement.case_against: The attribution remains the weak point and I do not want to hide it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed and Habener, who is not on the credited list, may have a comparable claim. Knudsen's design of long-acting analogues is what produced the drugs, so a discovery-side citation can look detached from the therapies in use. Any three-person cap leaves out someone with a substantial claim. Choosing the physiology and discovery side is a judgment about what this prize is for, and it is defensible, but it is a judgment and not a settled historical fact. If the documentary record on the active peptide could not support Mojsov, the committee would have to reconsider the third name, and I would then prefer to reopen the question openly instead of substituting the developer by default.

responses.point: Sandberg moved from Knudsen in her opening trio to Mojsov in round 1, but asked that the citation say explicitly that the prize recognises the route to therapy, so that omitting Knudsen is not read as dismissing drug development.
responses.response: I agree with the wording concern and have adopted it. My citation now states that the discoveries established the basis for incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity, so therapy is acknowledged as the consequence of the discovery while drug design is not credited. That wording does not name Knudsen, and I do not think we should pretend it does. I would not go further and add language about analogue design, because that would imply a credit the three names do not carry. I also take her implied point on Knudsen seriously: the choice of Mojsov over Knudsen is a statement about the kind of contribution the prize rewards, and the committee should own that statement.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius accepts discovery-versus-development as a framing but says it should not be a hard rule, since her own second choice, B036 (TNF blockade), was ranked highly because translation was the achievement.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge to my own consistency. I did not exclude translation as a category: I place B027 first because its discovery component and its clinical effect both sit within the credited names, which is not true of the TNF case, where the underlying TNF biology and antibody engineering lie outside Feldmann and Maini. I also remain unsure that TNF and IL-6 blockade are one achievement or two. That said, I have weighed her point about patient benefit and I keep B036 below B014 and B039 only narrowly. If B027 were to fail on attribution, I could support a clinically proven alternative, but I do not see it as a reason to add it as a second part this year.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that the unfolded protein response (B014) is a compact, thoroughly confirmed two-person prize but that its therapeutic payoff has not arrived, so it is a basic-science alternative to B027 and not a competitor.
responses.response: I agree with his assessment and it is why B014 stays first among my alternatives. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and the mechanism has been confirmed for decades, including links to diabetes and neurodegeneration. Where I now differ from my own earlier framing is that B014 would work only as a separate prize, not as a second part: Mori and Walter use two of the three places, and that leaves one for GLP-1, which would cut the incretin credit to a single name and misrepresent the work. So I treat B014 as the best candidate for a future year or as the fallback if B027 is blocked, and not as a way of enlarging this year's prize.

responses.point: Linnarsson notes that B014 is more natural as a second part alongside a clinically transformative achievement, and that B001 (SMN2 antisense) is a credible later candidate but narrow in breadth.
responses.response: I accept his critique of B001 and I have lowered it for this year: it rests on one disease target and one drug, competing SMA therapies exist, and the SMN gene work lies outside the credited names. On pairing B014 with B027 I see the logic in principle, but the three-person cap defeats it in practice, as described above. I would rather the committee state plainly that B014 is deferred than force a two-part configuration that gives GLP-1 a single laureate.

responses.point: El Manira prefers a physiology-only citation and says the committee should be explicit that it does not extend to drug design, which keeps the prize defensible if the historical record on the peptide is argued over.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and the citation is written accordingly, although I want it to retain the link to treatment so that it does not read as a prize for a hormone with no clinical consequence. I also share his caution about Habener: we cannot resolve the priority question from the supplied materials, and the committee should record that the configuration omits a contested contributor and not present the trio as uncontested. I disagree with him only on the sequence. If the record proved unsupportable for Mojsov, I would want a direct discussion of the third name, not an automatic fallback.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's documented priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be defended against Habener's claim, and whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third place. I cannot settle this from the supplied materials.
Whether a citation that links the discovery to treatment but credits only the discovery side is read by the wider public as a fair account of the therapies in use.
Whether B014 is better held for a future year than combined into this year's prize, given that the three-person cap leaves no workable second part.
I cannot independently verify the credit history or the chronology; my recollection is from the supplied candidate information.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal applies to any shortlisted candidate. For transparency: my documented co-authorship with Thomas Perlmann concerns dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy and involves no credited name, and my postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard does not involve any shortlisted candidate. Nothing in round 1 changed this disclosure.
